title: Choose Europe… or Are Research & Science Better Supported by Copyright Laws Elsewhere?
content:
Europe fails researchers in 7 cases.

Europe faces increasingly intense competition for research talent. The Choose Europe for Science initiative responds by helping attract and retain researchers and by promoting Europe’s strengths.

To improve Europe’s attractiveness compared to its competitors, decision-makers will also need to assess how we compare to other jurisdictions on copyright and how well Europe’s regime works for researchers.

There is still plenty to do!

Choosing Europe for science means choosing Europe for knowledge, too.

Click a case to expand. (Open all · Close all)

Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan and the US all allow TDM on legally accessed materials in partnership with industry, bringing extra resources to research institutions.

In the EU and UK, commercial partners are excluded. Researchers must buy an additional licence for content they already legally access, if one exists at all, and publisher contracts increasingly even try to block non-commercial TDM, against EU law.

title: Poison Pills
content:
Copyright reform is again on the horizon in Europe. Not only is the 2019 Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market under evaluation, but the European Commission has also called for evidence about a series of potential reforms and, just yesterday, 29 September, launched a targeted consultation.

One idea on the table is a possible reform of the Union’s copyright exception for research, to facilitate researchers’ work when engaging with copyrighted materials. There will be plenty of discussion about the precise wording of this in the months and years to come.

In this context, we will see the contours of a broader question: what are the aspects of copyright law that need to be avoided if we want to uphold the interests of users, the institutions they rely on, and society more broadly?

These legislative ‘poison pills’ sharply reduce the scope and beneficial impact of otherwise potentially beneficial legislative provisions. When engaging in copyright reform discussions, it is therefore valuable to look out for these and highlight the threat they pose early on.
